newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank says total deficits key to EMU entry.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank says total deficits key to EMU entry.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank on Wednesday made clear countries could not resolve the problems of trimming back budget deficits for European monetary union by simply ignoring extra costs resulting from economic weakness.

In its April monthly report, the central bank presented a model for assessing the structural components of a country's budget deficit, but warned that governments must continue to focus on the total shortfall.
"The financial total balance of state activities must remain the decisive measurement -- due also to its relevance for borrowing needs," the Bundesbank said.

The warning note from the Bundesbank comes as most European countries are undertaking a final, eleventh-hour drive to bring their deficits below three percent of gross domestic product to make sure they qualify for the single currency in 1999.
The budget deficit goal is one of a series of targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation and public debts which countries must meet this year to gain first-round entry to EMU.
For most countries it is also proving the hardest to reach.
The Bundesbank has already been openly critical of attempts by some nations to use special measures to reduce deficits this year by adding in special revenues or postponing outgoings.

But its study in this month's report also closed the door on the idea -- mooted by some -- that a recalculated deficit stripping out the impact of economic weakness or strength on budget spending should be used as the basis for the EMU test.

"According to the Maastricht treaty, this (the total deficit) is the measure which should be used as a basis for the examination of the question of whether the fiscal policy debt criterion is reached," the Bundesbank said.

Economic weakness tends to boost government spending as unemployment rises, placing a strain on welfare coffers and sometimes requiring stimulus packages, while on the income side tax receipts tend to fall due to the slower economic activity.

With the German economy currently in a sluggish recovery, a surge in jobless queues to record levels at the start of this year prompted economists to question whether Bonn had any chance of cutting 1996's 3.8 percent deficit far enough.
News expected next month on estimated tax receipts will be watched closely for signs as to whether the government forecast for a deficit of 2.9 percent of GDP this year is within reach.

Speaking to reporters on the way into a meeting of parliament's finance committee, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel once again squashed speculation that Germany will not be able to meet the target in time.
"We have the possibilty to meet the criteria. It all depends on growth," he told reporters, adding that the criteria should nonetheless be "stringently applied".
"3.0 is 3.0", is added, reiterating his precise definition of the Maastricht goal.

In the report, the Bundesbank said its study had showed that a worsening of 3-1/3 percentage points in Germany's deficit position between 1989 and 1996 was attributable to non-cyclical factors, such as higher debt servicing.
But it warned against overweighting such structural deficit calculations in the formulation of policy.

"Narrowing one's view to consider only the structural deficit brings with it the danger of underestimating the extent of a mistake on the fiscal policy front, particularly as the methods and statistical problems in calculating structural deficits have so far led to very different results or interpretations," the Bundesbank said.
